devotionals.title: This Day
devotionals.verseText:
This is the day that Yahweh has made;
let us rejoice and be glad in it.
devotionals.reflection:
Some mornings the day is already loud before your feet hit the floor. There is a list on the counter, and a message you have not answered. Joy feels like something you will get to later, once the work is done. Psalm 118 does not wait for a clear desk. It looks at this ordinary day, still messy and unfinished, and calls it made. Yahweh has made this one. He made the first morning of the world, and He made the days you still remember as easy. He has also made today.

You do not have to pretend you are cheerful about everything in it. This psalm is a song of thanks from someone who has already been in trouble. A few lines earlier the singer says, "I thank you that you answered me and have become my salvation." Then comes the line the church has long heard as a word about Jesus Christ: "The stone that the builders rejected has become the cornerstone." This is not a blank, easy day with nothing left to ask. Right after our verse the same voice still cries, "Please, Yahweh, save us!" and "Please, Yahweh, give us success!" So the gladness here is not a painted-on smile. It is a way of receiving the hours because the One who made them has also become our salvation in Jesus. There might be hard work in them. There might be a grief that sits in the room with you. The day is still His making, and you are still allowed to ask Him for help.

Think of standing at the kitchen sink with yesterday's dishes, looking at the date on the calendar as if it were only a deadline. The psalm would have you name that date as a gift first, a day made by the Father and held together by His Son. Say thank you for this day before you pick up the next task. Then walk into the hours as something Jesus has a share in, not as a test you have to pass. If you need to ask for rescue later in the same day, you are still inside the song, and the cornerstone still holds.
devotionals.prayer: Yahweh, You made this day, and I thank You for it before I know how it will go. I am crowded inside, and I want to rush past the morning. Thank You that Jesus Christ has become our salvation, the stone that the builders rejected, now the cornerstone. This day is Yours even when it looks ordinary. Give me a glad and steady heart. Help me receive these hours as a gift from You, not as a test I have to pass. When I stand at the sink or look at the calendar, remind me to say Your name first, and to remember Your Son. If the day turns hard, I will still come to You and ask for help, the way this psalm does. Please save me in what I cannot fix. We ask this by the blood of Jesus Christ and through His name we pray, amen.

devotionals.title: Where Help Comes From
devotionals.verseText:
My help comes from Yahweh,
the Maker of heaven and earth.
devotionals.reflection:
On a hard morning it is easy to look around and wonder where help is going to come from. Maybe a better plan, or a calmer mood. The psalm does not point there. It points to Yahweh, and then it tells you who He is: the Maker of heaven and earth. The hills in front of you may look huge. They are not the source. They were made. The One who made them is the help.

This is a song for the road, one of the psalms of ascents. It begins with a long look and a real question: "I lift my eyes to the mountains—" and then, "where does my help come from?" Travelers knew those hills could hide trouble, and some people also looked to high places for the wrong kind of help. The answer comes in our verse, and the next lines tell you what kind of help this is. "He will not let your foot slip;" and the One who guards Israel "neither dozes nor sleeps." That matters when help feels far away. The New Testament says of Jesus Christ, "Through him everything came to be; without him not a single thing came to be." The God who put the ground under your feet is not a stranger to the trouble standing on that same ground. Help in this psalm is not a wish tossed at the sky. It comes from Him, and in Jesus it has come near. He stays awake, and He stays with you.

Picture yourself in a parking lot outside a building you did not want to enter, staring up at the brick as if the size of it could save you. The psalm would lift your eyes one step farther, to the Maker, and to His Son. It is still right to ask a friend or a neighbor. It is still right to do the work of the day. Those things do not take the place of this sentence. When you do not know where to turn, you can say it simply: my help comes from Yahweh. Then stand up and go in, remembering that Jesus has said, "And remember, I am with you every day, until the end of the age." The One who made heaven and earth is watching over your going out and your coming in.
devotionals.prayer: Maker of heaven and earth, my help comes from You. I have been looking around for something large enough to hold me, and I need You to turn my eyes back to You, and to Jesus Christ, through whom everything came to be. Thank You that You do not doze, and that Your Son is with me every day. Stay near in the hard places of this day. Guard my steps when I feel like my foot could slip. Give me courage to walk into what is in front of me, without forgetting that the help itself comes from You. Watch over my going out and my coming in. I place this day, and the thing I am afraid to enter, in Your hands. We ask this by the blood of Jesus Christ and through His name we pray, amen.

devotionals.title: The Peace He Leaves With You
devotionals.verseText: Peace I leave you; my peace I give you; I give it not in the way the world gives. Let your hearts not be shaken, nor be fearful.
devotionals.reflection:
Jesus Christ says this on the night He tells His friends He is going away. They cannot see how the story turns out yet, and He does not pretend they are calm. Into that shaky room He puts a gift, and He is careful about what kind of gift it is. The world hands out peace when the news is good. It also shows up after a threat has passed, like a quiet house once everyone has finally gone to bed. That kind of peace walks out the door as soon as the hour does.

The peace He gives is His own. He does not promise that trouble will step aside first. These words come in the upper room, after a friend has asked why Jesus would show Himself to them and not to the world. Jesus has just promised them another Helper: "But the Advocate, the Holy Spirit, whom the Father will send in my name, he will teach you everything and remind you of everything I have said to you." Then He leaves them His peace. A moment later He says, "I go away, and I come to you." They are about to walk out toward the garden, and their hearts are already trembling. "Let your hearts not be shaken, nor be fearful" is not a scolding. He names the fear, and He answers it with what He gives: His own peace, on the way to the cross.

You may know a night like that. The house is finally still, but your chest is not, because tomorrow holds a hard conversation or a waiting room. You do not have to get everything quiet before you ask for this. Receive what Jesus leaves with you, and let it sit under the noise, like a floor you can stand on. He stayed with them in that room long enough to leave this gift, and He did not leave them alone. Ask for His peace tonight, and take it with you in the morning when you rise and go.
devotionals.prayer: Lord Jesus, You give a peace the world cannot lend and cannot take back. Some things in me are shaken tonight, and I do not want to pretend otherwise. Thank You that You did not leave Your friends with a speech and an empty room. You promised the Holy Spirit, and You left Your own peace with people who were already afraid. Meet my fear with that same peace. Let it sit under the noise of this day, even if the trouble does not step aside first. Remind me of Your words when my heart starts to tremble. Go with me into what is coming, and teach me to receive what You leave with me before I have made the house quiet. We ask this by the blood of Jesus Christ and through His name we pray, amen.

devotionals.title: Bring What You Carry
devotionals.verseText: Stop worrying about anything; in every situation, through prayer and requests with thanksgiving, bring your needs to God.
devotionals.reflection:
Paul writes this to friends in Philippi while he himself is in chains. He is not shaming anyone for having a need. He is telling you where a need belongs. "Stop worrying about anything" does not stand alone. It is joined right away to a practice: in every situation, through prayer and requests with thanksgiving, bring your needs to God. Worry is not told to vanish because you tried hard enough. It is given a place to go, and that place is the presence of the Lord who is near.

Look at the lines around it. Paul has just said, "The Lord is close at hand." The Lord he means is Jesus Christ, who is not far from a prison, and not far from your table. Then comes our verse, and right after it a promise: "And the peace of God, which surpasses all understanding, will guard your hearts and your minds in Christ Jesus." This is not advice from someone sitting at ease. Later in the same chapter Paul says he has learned to be content in want and in plenty. The thanksgiving he asks for does not cancel the need. It remembers that the One you are talking to has already been faithful in Jesus, and that memory changes the sound of the asking. A request that never says thank you can spin in circles at the kitchen table. A request held with thanks starts to feel like a conversation with Someone who is near.

Nothing is too small for "every situation". The bill on the counter. The talk you are dreading. You know how worry can circle at eleven at night, the same thought walking the same path. Name the need to the Father, through His Son. Thank God for one true thing. Leave it with Him. Paul could write this from a prison because the Lord was near to him there, not only after the chains came off. Then watch for the peace that guards your heart and mind in Christ Jesus, even if you have to come back in prayer before supper. That is still the practice this verse teaches us today.
devotionals.prayer: God, I bring You what I have been carrying, through Jesus Christ Your Son. Here is the need I can name, and here is my thanks for how You have already been faithful. I do not want to keep circling in worry at the table or in the dark. Thank You that the Lord is close at hand, and that Your peace can guard my heart and my mind in Christ Jesus. Teach me to leave this with You, and to come back in prayer as often as I need to. I give You the bill, the conversation I dread, and the thought that will not sit still. Guard me with Your peace, which is greater than my understanding. We ask this by the blood of Jesus Christ and through His name we pray, amen.

devotionals.title: The Treatment You Hope For
devotionals.verseText: Just as you want people to treat you, treat them in the same way.
devotionals.reflection:
This saying is short enough to keep in your pocket, and it can change the way a day goes. Jesus Christ does not start with a separate rule for every case. He starts with something you already know from the inside. You know how you hope to be treated when you are tired, or when you have made a mistake. You want a little patience. You want someone to hear you out. He takes that inner knowledge and turns it toward the person in front of you.

These words sit in a hard and generous stretch of teaching. Just before them Jesus says, "Love your enemies; treat well those who hate you". Just after them He asks what thanks is due if you only love the people who already love you. Then He says, "Be merciful, just as your Father is merciful." The treatment you hope for is not a soft way of avoiding the truth. It also does not mean staying quiet when a straight word is exactly what you would hope someone would give you. On a hard day, what most of us want is pretty simple: to be treated with dignity, and to be dealt with like a neighbor. Jesus takes that hope and makes it a way of life, because this is how He has treated us. He loved His enemies. He was merciful when we had no claim on mercy. The Golden Rule is not a thin politeness. It is the shape of His own heart, now asked of His people.

You do not have to feel fond of someone first. This can be practiced in one reply, or in who gets your patience in the checkout line, or in how you answer a short email that stung. Before you speak, remember how Jesus has treated you, and ask what you would hope for if the places were reversed. Then do that. That is harder than a general wish to be nice. It is a choice you can make in the next hour, with a real person, without waiting to feel ready. Mercy, in this teaching, looks like ordinary fairness offered to someone who may not offer it back, because Christ has already offered it to you.
devotionals.prayer: Lord Jesus, You know how I hope to be treated, and You have already treated me with a mercy I did not earn. Please give me that same patience and kindness toward the people I meet today, especially where it does not come easily. Thank You that the Father is merciful, and that You ask me to be merciful in the same way. I have been quick to answer from irritation. Slow me down in the checkout line, in the short email, in the little moments when I could choose dignity or scorn. Teach me to hear someone out the way I want to be heard. If a straight word is needed, help me give it the way I would hope to receive it. Let Your mercy set the pattern for mine. We ask this by the blood of Jesus Christ and through His name we pray, amen.

devotionals.title: Let It Shine Where You Live
devotionals.verseText: In the same way, your light must shine in front of others, so that they see the good you do and praise your Father in heaven.
devotionals.reflection:
A moment earlier, Jesus Christ has called His hearers the light of the world. A lamp, He says, belongs on the lampstand, not under a basket. Then He makes the picture practical. In the same way, your light must shine in front of others.

The words come in the Sermon on the Mount, right after the blessings and the saying about salt. Jesus tells them, "You are the light of the world. A town that sits on a hilltop cannot stay hidden." Then He adds, "Nor does anyone light a lamp and set it under a basket; they put it on the lampstand, and it gives light to everyone in the house." Our verse is the point of that picture. People should look at the good you do and praise your Father in heaven, not the person holding the lamp. This is not a push to be admired. The light is not yours first. It is His. Jesus is the Light, and He has set His people in the world so that ordinary goodness can be seen: a promise you actually keep, work done carefully when no one is scoring it, a quiet mercy nobody announced. None of this needs a crowd gathered on purpose. It needs to happen in the hallway or at the sink, in the places you already go, because that is where He has put the lamp.

If you have wondered whether a small faithfulness even matters, this verse says it does. Let it show where you are. If a neighbor is waiting on a promise, keep it. If you can do your work with care, do it that way even when the room is empty. A covered lamp helps no one, and a lamp waved for attention helps the wrong person. Keep the light where people actually live, not only where a speech can be made. The town on the hill is simply visible because of where it sits. Live that way in the life you already have. Then let the praise go to the Father who gave the light in Jesus, not back to you.
devotionals.prayer: Father in heaven, let the good You have placed in my care be seen for Your sake, not for mine. Do not let me hide it, and do not let me use it to gather praise for myself. Thank You that Jesus Christ has called His people light. Show me one place today where I have been covering what You meant to be seen: a promise I should keep, work I should do carefully, a mercy I could offer without making a speech. Give me courage to let it show in the hallway and at the sink. Keep my heart honest about why I do it. Let people see the good and thank You, and teach me to be glad when the praise goes to You and to Your Son. We ask this by the blood of Jesus Christ and through His name we pray, amen.

devotionals.title: Hope Enough to Spill
devotionals.verseText: Now may the God who gives hope fill you with every joy and peace as you believe, until hope overflows in you through the Holy Spirit’s power.
devotionals.reflection:
This is a blessing, and it names God by what He gives. He is the God who gives hope. That hope is not a guess that things might turn out fine. It is His gift, received as you trust Him, and it comes with joy and peace. Believing here does not mean every question is gone. It means you keep trusting while some questions are still open, because Jesus Christ is already the hope God has given.

Paul writes this near the end of a long appeal for unity. Jewish and Gentile believers in Rome have been learning how to share one life in Christ. A few lines earlier he says, "Welcome one another, therefore, just as Christ also welcomed you, for the glory of God." He then gathers old promises about the nations, ending with this: "There will be a shoot from the root of Jesse, one who stands up to govern the nations; the nations will place their hope in him." That shoot is Jesus. Then comes our blessing. The overflowing hope is not a private comfort you have to clutch in your pocket. It is meant to spill, the way a welcome spills toward people who used to stand outside, because Christ has already welcomed you. And because the overflow is the Spirit's work, you do not have to squeeze it out of an empty heart.

Ask for the blessing the way it is written. Then watch for one place today where a little of that hope in Jesus can spill over. You might sit with a tired friend at the kitchen table, or stay with someone in a waiting room, without having a fix to offer. A word you did not have to say, or simply staying, can be enough. Paul wanted a church in which people who used to stand far apart could share one hope. If hope only stays inside one heart, it has not yet done all that this blessing asks. True hope that comes from God in Christ is able to travel from one person to another.
devotionals.prayer: God who gives hope, fill me with joy and peace as I trust You. Let hope overflow, by the power of Your Holy Spirit, toward someone who needs it today. Thank You that You welcomed us in Jesus Christ, and that the nations are invited to place their hope in Him. Make me a person who welcomes, not only a person who receives. I think of the people who are tired, and of the rooms where someone is waiting for news. Give me a hope that can spill in those places: a word, a visit, a willingness to stay. Guard me from clutching what You give as if it were only for me. I receive Your joy and Your peace. We ask this by the blood of Jesus Christ and through His name we pray, amen.

devotionals.title: When You Are Weighed Down
devotionals.verseText: “Come to me, all who are weary and weighed down, and I will give you rest.
devotionals.reflection:
You can be tired in more than one way at once. The body is worn down, and then there is the other weight, the kind you carry in your chest after a long stretch of being needed. Some evenings you come in from a late shift with your coat still on, and you stand in the hallway because sitting down feels like you might not get back up. Jesus Christ speaks into that kind of hour. "Come to me, all who are weary and weighed down, and I will give you rest."

He says this after praying to the Father. He has just said, "None knows the Son fully except the Father; none knows the Father fully except the Son, and anyone to whom the Son is pleased to make him known." The invitation is not a slogan for people who already feel spiritual. It comes from the One who can actually make the Father known, and who sees people worn thin by work and worry, and by a kind of religion that never lets them breathe. The next lines keep the same welcome. He says, "Take my yoke upon you and learn from me, for I am gentle and humble in heart, and you will find rest for your souls." Then, "For my yoke is kindly and my load is light." A yoke still means there is work to do, and a load still has to be carried. But He is gentle, and He does not pile a heavier burden on the one you already have. Rest, in His mouth, is a gift He gives, not a prize you earn once the list is finished. He would soon carry the heaviest load of all, and this is the rest He offers before He does.

So come as you are tonight. You do not have to get the kitchen settled first, or catch up on the messages, or explain why you are this tired. Stand in the hallway if that is where you are, and come to Jesus there. Tell Him you are weary. Tell Him what is weighing you down, even if the words come out plain and short. Then receive the rest He offers, if only for the next hour, and let tomorrow's work wait until morning. The invitation is still for you, and it has not expired because the day ran long.
devotionals.prayer: Jesus, I come to You tired. I am weary in my body, and I am weighed down in ways I do not always know how to name. Thank You that You invite people like me, and that You are pleased to make the Father known. I do not want to wait until I feel caught up before I come. Meet me in the hallway, and in the hours when sitting down feels like too much. Give me the rest You promised. Teach me to take Your kindly yoke and to leave the heavier load I keep trying to carry alone. Stay with me tonight, and help me sleep as someone who has been welcomed by You, not as someone who still has to prove that I am allowed to stop. We ask this by the blood of Jesus Christ and through His name we pray, amen.

devotionals.title: The Steps You Did Not Plan
devotionals.verseText:
A man’s heart plans his way,
but Yahweh directs his steps.
devotionals.reflection:
You can start a Saturday with a neat list and still lose the afternoon in ten minutes. The list is on the back of an envelope: the errand, the visit, the hour you meant to keep quiet. Then a call comes, or a child gets sick, or the bus never shows, and the day you planned is gone. You may still be standing there with the envelope in your hand, looking at a schedule that no longer matches the clock. "A man’s heart plans his way, but Yahweh directs his steps."

The proverb does not scold you for planning. A heart that plans is doing something human and often wise. The saying sits among other lines about ordinary life, about work and fairness and the way a person tries to find a path. What it will not let you do is treat the plan as if it were the last word. Yahweh directs the steps, including the ones that turn away from your outline. Jesus Christ is that Lord of the path. He said, "I am the way, and the truth, and the life." Nobody comes to the Father except through Him. His own steps were directed by the Father, even when the path led to a cross He had spoken of in advance. That can feel like interruption in our smaller days, and sometimes it is a mercy you only recognize later. Other times the redirected step is simply hard, and you are asked to trust the One who is still directing while you do not yet see why. The comfort is not that every change will feel good. The comfort is that your life is not only in your own hands, because it is in His.

So make your list. Write it down if that helps you begin. Then hold it loosely enough that a changed hour does not have to feel like a failure. When the call comes and the afternoon turns, ask Jesus to direct the next step, not only the one you had already chosen. You might need to sit with someone longer than you meant to. You might need to take a later bus and use the wait to pray. You can even bless the redirected step before you understand it. The day can still belong to Him when it no longer belongs to your envelope.
devotionals.prayer: Yahweh, I am good at planning, and I am not always good at being redirected. Thank You that I can make a list, and that You direct my steps even when the day comes apart. Thank You for Jesus Christ, who is the way, and whose own steps were in Your hands all the way to the cross. Teach me not to treat my outline as if it were sacred. Direct the step I did not expect. Give me a willing heart when the afternoon changes, and keep me from bitterness when I lose the quiet hour I wanted. I trust You with the way I had mapped, and with the way I am actually walking. Lead me in it, through Your Son. We ask this by the blood of Jesus Christ and through His name we pray, amen.

devotionals.title: Take Thought for One Another
devotionals.verseText: And let us take thought for one another, how to stir each other up to love and good works,
devotionals.reflection:
It is easy to go through a Sunday as if you were only there for yourself. You find a seat, you listen, you leave as soon as the last word is said, and the people around you stay a little blurry. You may even mean well, and still make it all the way to the door without having looked anyone in the eye. The writer of Hebrews will not let love stay that vague. "And let us take thought for one another, how to stir each other up to love and good works,"

That line does not float free. Just before it, the writer has been speaking of Jesus Christ. "So then, brothers, since by Jesus’ blood we have boldness to go into the holy place," we are told to come near, and then, "Let us keep hold of the hope we confess without wavering, for the one who gave the promise can be trusted." Hope belongs in your own chest because Jesus has opened the way, and it is also meant to turn into care for the people beside you. The next sentence urges them not to give up meeting together, because some already had. This was a community under pressure, tempted to drift, and the writer is after more than a scolding about attendance for its own sake. He wants a way of staying near enough to wake love up in each other when it starts to sleep, because we have been brought near by Jesus’ blood. Stirring is an active word. It assumes that love and good works can settle, and that they need a friend to rouse them. You may need that rousing yourself more often than you like to admit.

After you leave the service, or if you could not get there at all, take thought for one person. It might be the empty chair you noticed, or a name that has been quiet on your phone. Send the message, or stay long enough to ask how the week really was, and then stay for the answer. You do not have to stir a whole room at once. Thoughtful love usually starts with one name, and with the hope you are still holding because Jesus has made a way, and the One who promised can be trusted.
devotionals.prayer: Lord Jesus, teach me to take thought for someone besides myself. I can walk in and walk out and barely see the people next to me. Thank You that by Your blood we have boldness to come near, and that the One who gave the promise can be trusted. Show me the person I should notice today, the empty chair or the quiet name. Give me the courage to send the message, or to stay and listen. Stir up love and good works in me, and let me be a friend who rouses them in someone else. Keep me from drifting. Hold me near Your people, and make my care more than a vague wish. We ask this by the blood of Jesus Christ and through His name we pray, amen.

devotionals.title: Peace When the World Is Heavy
devotionals.verseText: I have told you these things so that in me you may have peace. In the world you have distress; but take courage: I have conquered the world.”
devotionals.reflection:
Monday can arrive before you are ready for it. You open the inbox while the coffee is still too hot to drink, and the week's trouble is already waiting in a stack of subject lines. Some of them can wait. A few of them cannot, and your stomach knows the difference before your mind has caught up. Jesus Christ knew His friends were about to walk into a hard stretch, and He did not pretend otherwise. "I have told you these things so that in me you may have peace. In the world you have distress; but take courage: I have conquered the world."

He says this on the night before the cross. A sentence earlier He tells them the hour is coming when they will be scattered, each to his own, and He will be left alone. Then He adds, "And yet I am not by myself, for the Father is with me." The peace He offers does not depend on a calm schedule. He gives peace in Him, while distress is still real in the world. He does not tell them to deny the distress. He tells them to take courage because He has already conquered the world they are afraid of. By morning He will be on His way to the cross, and this is the courage He leaves in the room.

You can carry that into the inbox. The messages may still be there, and some of them may be heavy. You do not have to find a peaceful world first. You can ask Jesus for peace in Him before you answer the first one, and again when a subject line lands like a stone. Take courage, not because Monday is easy, but because He has conquered what feels so large in front of you. The Father was with Him in that night, and you are not walking into this week as someone He has left alone.
devotionals.prayer: Jesus, I need the peace that is found in You. The world in front of me already feels heavy, and Monday has a way of arriving before I am ready. Thank You that You told Your friends the truth, and that You have conquered the world. I believe the Father was with You that night, and I ask You not to leave me alone in this week. Give me peace before I open the first message, and again when the distress rises. Help me take courage, not because the work is light, but because You have already overcome what I fear. Stay with me in the inbox, and in every hour that feels like too much. We ask this by the blood of Jesus Christ and through His name we pray, amen.

devotionals.title: The Word You Send Back
devotionals.verseText:
A gentle answer turns back rage,
but a word that wounds stirs up anger.
devotionals.reflection:
A sharp message can set your whole body on edge. You feel it in your chest, and your thumb hovers over the reply, already writing the sentence that will make the other person feel it too. The draft is half done before you have even decided to send it, and the sharp edge of it is already there. The proverb names that fork in the road with almost no decoration. "A gentle answer turns back rage, but a word that wounds stirs up anger."

This is how the chapter opens, among sayings about speech. The next line says, "Knowledge sounds good from a wise tongue;" and then, "folly bubbles from the mouths of fools." The point is close to the ground. Words do something. They can cool a room, or they can throw fuel on a fire that was already too hot. A gentle answer is not another word for a weak one. It does not mean you have to accept what is false, or laugh off what hurt you. It means you do not have to add a wound to the wound. Rage often comes looking for a partner. The proverb says you do not have to volunteer.

Jesus Christ is our pattern here. He could have answered His accusers with a cutting word, and He chose a different way. He told the truth without reaching for the sharp edge we reach for so quickly. When we ask for a gentle answer, we are asking to speak as He did. Before you send the reply, wait long enough to take a breath. If you need to walk to the sink, or step outside the door, do that first. Ask Him for a gentle answer, especially if you feel justified in writing a cutting one. You might still need to tell the truth, and you can do that without aiming to bruise.
devotionals.prayer: Yahweh, You hear the words I have not sent yet. You know how quickly I can answer from a hurt place, and how ready I am to wound when I have been wounded. Thank You for this proverb, which tells the truth about what speech can do. Give me a gentle answer today, the kind of word Jesus Christ would give. Slow my thumb, and slow my mouth, especially when I feel I am in the right. If I need to tell the truth, help me tell it without aiming to bruise. Keep me from adding fuel to a fire that is already too hot. I ask for a cool spirit and a clean word, and I trust You with the conversation I cannot finish on my own. We ask this by the blood of Jesus Christ and through His name we pray, amen.

devotionals.title: Forget None of His Kindnesses
devotionals.verseText:
Bless Yahweh, my soul,
and forget none of his kindnesses—
devotionals.reflection:
A Wednesday can go by in a blur of dishes and small tasks, and by evening you may feel as if nothing worth naming has happened. The calendar is almost at the end of the week, and your mind may already be running ahead to tomorrow's plans. The psalm will not let your soul skip the blessing that belongs to this day first. "Bless Yahweh, my soul, and forget none of his kindnesses—"

The singer starts by talking to himself. "Bless Yahweh, my soul, and all that is within me, bless his holy name!" Then he begins a list, not of his own achievements, but of what Yahweh has done. He is the one "who pardons every one of your iniquities, who cures every one of your sicknesses," and "who buys back your life from the pit," then "who sets a crown on you of covenant love and compassion," He places that crown on the person who might have forgotten. He is not asking you to invent a good mood. He is calling you to remember, because forgetting is easy when the day has been ordinary, and because kindness already given can slip out of view.

The greatest of those kindnesses is Jesus Christ. In Him, God pardons iniquity and buys a life back from the pit, not as an idea, but as a Person who came near. When you clear the table tonight, name a few of those kindnesses out loud, even if you are the only one in the room. Pardon if you needed it. A body that made it through the day. A meal, or a person who still loves you. And the Son, who is the kindness you must not forget. Bless Him with what is in you, and refuse to treat His gifts as if they were only background. Tomorrow may bring a fuller table for some of us, but the kindnesses are already here, and they are worth remembering before the day closes.
devotionals.prayer: Yahweh, I bless Your holy name. I do not want to forget Your kindnesses, especially on a day that felt ordinary. Thank You that You pardon iniquity, and that in Jesus Christ You have bought back lives from the pit. Thank You for covenant love and compassion I did not earn. As I clear the table, help me name what You have already given: the meal, the strength to get through the hours, the people You have set near me, and Your Son. Teach my soul to bless You, not only when the day feels large. Keep me from rushing past Your gifts as if they were only background. I remember Your kindness tonight, and I thank You for it. We ask this by the blood of Jesus Christ and through His name we pray, amen.

devotionals.title: Thanks in Whatever Happens
devotionals.verseText: whatever happens, give thanks; this is what God wills for you in Christ Jesus.
devotionals.reflection:
Thanksgiving Day can arrive with a full kitchen and a tight heart at the same time. There may be an empty chair. There may be a dish that did not turn out, or a quiet worry about money that does not go away because the calendar says to be grateful. The room can be loud with talk and still hold a silence no one quite names, a tightness sitting under the conversation. Paul writes to a young church, "whatever happens, give thanks; this is what God wills for you in Christ Jesus."

He sets that line in a short string of counsel: "Rejoice always," then "pray without ceasing," and then this call to thanks. Paul is not asking you to enjoy every circumstance, or to pretend a hard year has been easy. The thanks is "whatever happens," and it is God's will for you in Christ Jesus, which means it is lived from a life already held by Him. The Thessalonians knew distress. They also knew the Lord Jesus. Thanks, in that setting, is a way of staying turned toward God when the day is mixed, and when joy and prayer have to share the table with sorrow. You can tell the truth about the ache and still speak thanks without lying, because your life is held in Christ.

If you sit down to a meal today, you can tell the truth about what is missing and still give thanks for what is there. Say the names of the people present. Thank God for the food, and for Christ Jesus, in whom this will of God has been given to you. He is the reason thanks is possible on a mixed day, not because the ache has vanished, but because He has not. If the gathering is small, or if you are eating alone, the verse is still yours. Whatever happens includes this table, this year, this ache, and the goodness that has not been canceled by any of it.
devotionals.prayer: Father, whatever happens, I want to give thanks, because this is Your will for me in Christ Jesus. Some parts of this day are glad, and some parts are tight in my chest. Thank You for the Lord Jesus, who holds my life when the year has been hard. Thank You for the food, and for the people at the table, and even for the honesty of an empty chair. Teach me to rejoice, to pray without ceasing, and to keep my face turned toward You. I do not have to pretend the sorrow is not here. I can still thank You in the middle of a mixed day. Receive my thanks, and sit with us at this table. We ask this by the blood of Jesus Christ and through His name we pray, amen.

devotionals.title: New Every Morning
devotionals.verseText: they are new every morning; great is your faithfulness.
devotionals.reflection:
The day after a big holiday has its own kind of quiet. The dishes are mostly done, the leftovers are stacked in the fridge, and the house feels a little emptier than it did yesterday. Maybe you are tired. Maybe the gathering stirred up old hurts you thought were settled, or reminded you of how much has changed. Mornings like this can feel heavy before you even get out of bed. Into that kind of morning comes a line from one of the saddest books in the Bible: "they are new every morning; great is your faithfulness."

Lamentations was written after Jerusalem fell. The city was burned, the temple was in ruins, and people were starving in the streets. The poet does not hide any of it. Most of the book is grief, written line after line in careful patterns, as if the only way to hold that much sorrow was to give it a shape. Then, right in the middle of the third poem, the writer turns. He remembers that Yahweh's steadfast love does not stop and that His mercies do not run out. And then he says they are new every morning.

I love that this hope is not found in a happy book. It was written by someone standing in rubble. He did not wait for the city to be rebuilt before he could say God was faithful. He said it with ash still on the ground. That tells me I do not have to wait until my life is in order to trust the mercy of God. His faithfulness is not a reward for a tidy week. It is something He brings fresh each day, and it comes to us most clearly in Jesus Christ. His mercies really are new, and the morning of His resurrection is the proof that they do not run out.

So this morning, whatever is left over from yesterday, you get a new portion of mercy in Him. Not yesterday's mercy warmed up again, but today's. You can take a slow breath, pour your coffee, and tell Him out loud that His faithfulness is great. Then take the next small step. He will meet you in it, and tomorrow morning He will be there with mercy again.
devotionals.prayer: Yahweh, thank You that Your mercies are new every morning, and that they meet me in Jesus Christ. Yesterday is behind me, with its joys and its sore spots, and I bring all of it to You. Some mornings I wake up already tired, and I forget that You have not changed overnight. Remind me that Your faithfulness is great, even when my strength is small and the house feels empty. I do not need to fix everything before I come to You. Give me today's portion of mercy, and help me to take it the way Your people gathered manna, one day at a time. Let me walk through this ordinary morning trusting that You are already here. Thank You for loving me again today. We ask this by the blood of Jesus Christ and through His name we pray, amen.

devotionals.title: When You Are Tired of Doing Good
devotionals.verseText: We must not tire of doing what is right, for when the time comes we shall reap, if we do not lose heart.
devotionals.reflection:
Some kinds of goodness are slow and unseen. You visit your mother in the nursing home every Saturday, even when she does not remember you came. You keep paying down a debt a little at a time. You keep praying for a son who has not spoken to you in two years. You keep showing up to a small church where the same eight people sit in the same pews. None of it makes the news, and some weeks it feels like none of it makes a difference. Paul has a word for people in that place: "We must not tire of doing what is right, for when the time comes we shall reap, if we do not lose heart."

Paul wrote this near the end of his letter to the churches in Galatia. He had just told them to carry one another's burdens and reminded them that people reap what they sow. He was writing to ordinary believers who were being pulled in many directions, some of them worn out by arguments and pressure. He does not tell them the work will be easy. He tells them it will not be wasted, because it is held by Jesus Christ.

Anyone who has ever grown a garden knows this. You put seeds in the ground in spring, water them, pull weeds in the heat, and for weeks there is almost nothing to show for it. Then one day there are tomatoes. The harvest was never in your control, but your faithfulness in the dirt still mattered. God is the One who brings the harvest, and He is not late, even when we feel that He is. Jesus Himself did not tire of doing what was right. He went all the way to the cross, and the harvest of that obedience is sure. That is why we can keep going.

If you are tired today, it is okay to admit it. Being tired is not the same as giving up. Rest if you need to. Ask for help. But do not quit the good thing God has put in your hands. "When the time comes" is in His calendar, not ours, and He sees every quiet act of love you have done. Not one of them is lost with Him.
devotionals.prayer: Lord, I am tired. You know the good things I have been trying to do, and You know how small the results look right now. I confess that I have wanted to quit more than once this month. Thank You for the promise that when the time comes, there will be a harvest, and thank You for Jesus Christ, who did not lose heart. Help me not to lose heart. Give me rest where I need rest, and give me friends to help me carry what is heavy. Keep my hands busy with the good work You have given me, and keep my eyes on You instead of on the results. I trust You with the timing. You see what no one else sees, and You are faithful to finish what You start. We ask this by the blood of Jesus Christ and through His name we pray, amen.

devotionals.title: Waiting with My Whole Soul
devotionals.verseText:
I wait for Yahweh; my whole soul waits,
and I put my hope in his word.
devotionals.reflection:
Today many churches begin Advent, the four weeks before Christmas when Christians remember the long wait for the Messiah and look ahead to His return. Advent is a season about waiting, and most of us are not very good at it. We refresh the tracking page for a package three times a day. We sit in the doctor's office reading the same poster on the wall over and over. Waiting makes us restless because it reminds us that we are not in charge. The psalmist knew that feeling well: "I wait for Yahweh; my whole soul waits, and I put my hope in his word."

Psalm 130 is one of the Songs of Ascents, short psalms that pilgrims sang as they walked up to Jerusalem for the festivals. It begins in the depths, with a person crying out from a very low place, aware of sin and in need of mercy. The psalm does not pretend things are fine. But it moves from the depths toward hope, and the turning point is this verse. The writer is waiting, and he is waiting with all of himself.

Notice that he does not just wait for something to happen. He waits for Yahweh. There is a difference between waiting for a result and waiting for a Person. When you wait for a result, you watch the clock. When you wait for someone you love, you watch the door. Israel waited centuries for God's promises to be fulfilled, and then, in a small town, Jesus Christ was born. God kept His word in a way no one expected. The same Jesus will come again, and Advent looks both ways, back to the manger and forward to His return.

This Advent, maybe you are waiting on something too: a diagnosis, a job, a reconciliation, a prayer that has been sitting unanswered for a long time. You do not have to pretend that waiting is easy. But you can turn it toward Him. Put your hope in His word, not in the timetable you would have chosen. He has never once failed to keep His promises, and He will not start with you.
devotionals.prayer: Yahweh, I wait for You. My whole soul waits, and I put my hope in Your word. You know how impatient I can be, and how quickly I start watching the clock instead of watching for You. As Advent begins, teach me to wait the way Your people waited for the Messiah, with hope that does not give up. I bring You the things I am waiting on right now, the answers I have not received and the doors that have not opened. I lay them in Your hands. Thank You that You kept Your promise when Jesus Christ was born. Help me trust that You will keep every promise You have made to me. Come, Lord Jesus. We ask this by the blood of Jesus Christ and through His name we pray, amen.

devotionals.title: Hope, Hold, Persist
devotionals.verseText: Rejoice in hope, hold firm in affliction, persist in prayer.
devotionals.reflection:
Some Bible verses are long and winding, and some are short enough to fit on a sticky note on your bathroom mirror. This is one of the short ones: "Rejoice in hope, hold firm in affliction, persist in prayer." Three little commands, each only a few words long, and yet plenty of people have lived on this verse for years.

Paul wrote it in the part of Romans where he turns from teaching to everyday life. After eleven chapters about God's mercy in Christ, he says, in effect, here is what that mercy looks like when you live it out. He talks about loving one another, serving, sharing with people in need, and welcoming strangers. Tucked in the middle is this little rhythm of hope, endurance, and prayer, all of it held together by Jesus Christ.

Picture a woman caring for her husband through a long illness. Her days are full of medications, appointments, and nights of interrupted sleep. If you asked how she keeps going, she might point to these words and say, "I rejoice in what's coming, I hang on for today, and I keep talking to God about all of it." She would not say it is easy. She would say it is enough.

Notice that rejoicing comes first, and it is joy in hope, not joy in circumstances. Her circumstances are hard. Her hope is in Christ, who has promised resurrection and a day without tears. That hope makes the hard days bearable. Then comes holding firm, which is a plain word for endurance. Then prayer, not once, but persistent, like a child who keeps tugging at a parent's sleeve.

You might not be facing anything as heavy as she is. Or you might be facing something heavier. Either way, these three commands can steady you this week. Find one thing to rejoice in about what God has promised in His Son. Hold on through today's hard part. And keep praying, even if your prayers feel like the same words over and over. God does not get tired of hearing from you.
devotionals.prayer: Father, help me to rejoice in hope today. My circumstances are not all happy, but You have promised me a future in Christ, and nothing can take that away. Help me to hold firm in the trouble I am facing, one hour at a time. And help me keep praying, even when I feel like I am saying the same thing again and again. Thank You that You never grow tired of listening. Strengthen people I know who are caring for someone sick, or carrying a long burden alone. Give them hope, endurance, and the steady comfort of Your presence. Teach me to live this verse not only on good days, but on the hard ones too. We ask this by the blood of Jesus Christ and through His name we pray, amen.

devotionals.title: Good News for Everyone
devotionals.verseText: The angel said to them, “Have no fear. See, I am announcing to you good news of a great joy, which is for the whole people.
devotionals.reflection:
Shepherds were not the people you invited to dinner in first century Judea. Their work kept them outside with the animals, often at night, and they were not always trusted. They smelled like sheep. So it is surprising, and a little wonderful, that the first announcement of Jesus Christ's birth went to them. An angel appeared in the dark fields outside Bethlehem, and the shepherds were terrified. Luke tells it this way: "The angel said to them, “Have no fear. See, I am announcing to you good news of a great joy, which is for the whole people."

Notice the order. First, "Have no fear." God knew how frightened they were, and His first word through the angel was comfort. Then came the news itself: good news, great joy, and it was for the whole people. Not just for priests in the temple or for the important families in Jerusalem, but for everyone, including working men on a cold hillside. The joy is Jesus Himself, a Savior born for people who would never have put themselves first in line.

We are now in the season when stores start playing Christmas music and the lights go up on houses. It is easy to think that Christmas belongs to people whose lives look like greeting cards. But the first Christmas announcement went to people on the edges. If you feel like an outsider this season, if you are working nights, or living alone, or wondering if you belong in church, the angel's message was meant for people like you first.

Think about the clerk working the overnight shift at a gas station, or the nurse who spends the holiday on a hospital floor. For many people like that, the holidays are the loneliest time of year. God chose to announce His Son's birth to people working the night shift. That is not an accident. It is the heart of the gospel.

So whatever you are carrying into December, hear the angel's first words. Have no fear. There is good news, and it is for you, because Jesus Christ has come.
devotionals.prayer: Lord God, thank You for sending good news of great joy to the shepherds in the field. Thank You that Your first word to them was "Have no fear." I need to hear that today too. Some of my fears are loud, and some are quiet, but You see all of them. Thank You that the news of Jesus Christ is for the whole people, for the lonely and the overlooked, for those working nights and those sitting by themselves. Let me receive that news again this December as if for the first time. Help me to share it with someone who feels left out of the season. Fill my heart with the joy that comes from knowing Your Son came for me. We ask this by the blood of Jesus Christ and through His name we pray, amen.

devotionals.title: He Finishes What He Starts
devotionals.verseText: I am confident of this very thing, that the one who began a good work in you will carry it through to its finish, right up to the day of Christ Jesus.
devotionals.reflection:
Many of us have a drawer full of projects we started and never finished. A sweater with one sleeve. A notebook with the first three pages of a journal. A book about learning Spanish with a bookmark stuck in chapter two. Maybe you have a drawer like that too. We are all good at beginnings. Finishing is harder. That is why this verse is such a comfort: "I am confident of this very thing, that the one who began a good work in you will carry it through to its finish, right up to the day of Christ Jesus."

Paul wrote these words from prison. He was in chains, not sure whether he would live or die, and yet his letter to the church in Philippi is one of the most joyful things he ever wrote. He remembered how that church had started, with a businesswoman named Lydia by a river and a jailer whose family was baptized in the middle of the night. He had watched God start something there, and he was sure God would not leave it half done.

The confidence Paul has is not in the Philippians. It is in God, and it looks toward the day of Christ Jesus. People quit. People get distracted, discouraged, and tired. But God does not leave work unfinished. When He begins something in a person, whether it is faith, or healing, or a new way of loving others, He intends to bring it all the way to completion, and that finish line is the day of His Son.

That is a comfort when you look at yourself and see how far you still have to go. Maybe you are still impatient, still struggling with an old habit, still more afraid than you want to be. It is easy to think you are a disappointment. But you are not a project God has stuffed in a drawer. He is still working, and Jesus Christ will not leave you halfway done.

So be patient with yourself today, because God is patient with you. Keep showing up. The One who started this good work in you is not going to stop halfway.
devotionals.prayer: Father, thank You for the good work You began in me. I can see so many unfinished places in my life, things I wish were different by now. Sometimes I get discouraged and think You must be tired of me. But Your word says You will carry Your work through to its finish, right up to the day of Christ Jesus. I choose to trust that today. Thank You that You do not quit on Your people. Help me to be patient with myself the way You are patient with me. Keep shaping me, even in the slow and hidden places. And let me see the people around me as Your unfinished work too, loved and still growing. We ask this by the blood of Jesus Christ and through His name we pray, amen.

devotionals.title: Whom Shall I Fear?
devotionals.reflection:
It gets dark early in December. Around here, by a little after four in the afternoon the sky is already fading, and by five it feels like the middle of the night. Long dark evenings can do something to a person. Worries seem bigger after sunset. Small fears grow teeth. That is why I like reading this psalm at this time of year: "Yahweh is my light and my salvation; whom shall I fear? Yahweh is the stronghold of my life; of whom shall I be afraid?"

Psalm 27 is a psalm of David, and David knew real danger. He was chased by King Saul, hunted in the wilderness, and later betrayed by his own son. When he asks, "whom shall I fear?", he is not pretending there are no enemies. Later in the psalm he talks openly about armies and false witnesses. But he has decided where his confidence will rest. Yahweh is his light, so the darkness does not get the last word. Yahweh is his stronghold, a fortress, a safe place high above the danger.

That light and that salvation have a name. Jesus Christ is the light God has given us, and He is our salvation. He walked into the dark and was not overcome by it. I think of a child who wakes up from a nightmare and calls for her father. He comes in and turns on the light, and suddenly the shadows in the corner are just a coat hanging on a chair. The fear did not leave because the room changed. It left because her father came and turned on the light. That is what God does for us in His Son. He does not always remove the hard things, but He shows us that we are not alone with them.

Maybe your fears this week are about money, or health, or a family member who is struggling. Name them honestly. Then ask David's question out loud. Whom shall I fear? If Yahweh is your light in Jesus Christ, the dark is not as strong as it feels. If He is your stronghold, you have a place to run. Tonight, when the sun goes down early, let that be your reminder that He is still your light.
devotionals.prayer: Yahweh, You are my light and my salvation, and I see that light in Jesus Christ. You are the stronghold of my life. When the evenings are long and my worries grow in the dark, remind me that You are near. I bring You the fears I carry tonight, about my family, my health, my money, and my future. I do not want to pretend they are not there, but I do not want them to rule me either. Turn on the light in the corners of my heart where fear hides. Be my safe place, my fortress, my refuge. Help me to answer David's question with his confidence. Whom shall I fear? With You beside me, I will not be afraid. Thank You for holding me. We ask this by the blood of Jesus Christ and through His name we pray, amen.
